research.summary: Ranked-choice general with one Democrat and three Republicans. Kreiss-Tomkins leads every poll on first choices, but in two of the three the Republicans together have more first choices than he does.
points: First choices: Alaska Survey Research (Oct 1 to 3) Kreiss-Tomkins 48, Wilson 27, Bronson 15, Taylor 10; NYT/Siena (Sep 24 to Oct 1) 40, 20, 15, 11; Cygnal (R, Sep 24 to 27) 44, 24, 8, 9.
Cook moved the race to Lean D on Oct 13. Hours later Trump endorsed Wilson at a Wasilla rally and called Bronson and Taylor lesser candidates, a push to consolidate Republican rankings.
At the Oct 8 debate Bronson and Taylor said they would rank each other second and Wilson third.
Main issues: the Permanent Fund dividend and a roughly $2 billion structural deficit, education funding, data centers. Ballot Measure 2 would repeal ranked-choice voting.
research.ballot: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins (D), Bernadette Wilson (R), Dave Bronson (R), Treg Taylor (R); ranked-choice. Tom Begich (D) withdrew and endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins.
research.adjustment_reason: Every poll is first choice only, so none shows the final round, and Trump's push to consolidate the Republican vote came after Cook's move to Lean D. Moved 1.5 points toward the Republicans.

sources.title: Alaska Beacon: Trump endorses Wilson at Alaska rally (Oct 14)

research.summary: Hobbs has led every public poll, by as much as 17 points, against a Biggs campaign closely tied to Trump.
points: HighGround (released Oct 13): Hobbs +17. The Biggs campaign disputes it because the pollster's firm works for a group funding pro-Hobbs ads.
Noble Predictive Insights (Aug 10 to 13): Hobbs +13 with 12% undecided; Noble expects the race to tighten to single digits.
Hobbs won in 2022 by 17,117 votes. Early voting began Oct 7.

research.summary: Donalds leads, with a seven to one money advantage, but the latest poll has the race inside the margin of error.
points: UNF (Oct 12 to 19, 1,471 likely voters): Donalds 49, Jolly 47, narrowed from Donalds +5 in July. Mason-Dixon (Sep 28 to Oct 1): Donalds 48, Jolly 41.
Donalds has raised more than $140 million against about $20 million for Jolly. Jolly declined all debates.
Main issues: property insurance and property taxes, Amendment 3 on the homestead exemption, data centers.
research.ballot: Byron Donalds (R), David Jolly (D), Scott Eckhard Jewett (L), five independents.

research.summary: A dead heat. Jackson has far more money and Kemp's backing; Democrats are markedly more enthusiastic.
points: AJC/UGA (Oct 7 to 15, 1,000 likely voters): Jackson 46, Bottoms 45, 8% undecided. Independents lean Bottoms 43 to 38.
68% of Democrats say they are very enthusiastic to vote, against 48% of Republicans.
Jackson spent at least $108 million of his own money in the primary and dominates TV. Kemp, at about 70% approval, backs him; Jackson skipped Trump's Macon rally.

sources.title: AJC: Jackson has outspent Bottoms, but Democratic enthusiasm has the race knotted

research.summary: Open seat. Sand leads in every October poll and has far more cash for the final weeks.
points: Emerson (Oct 5 to 6): Sand 49, Lahn 45. Marist (Oct 8 to 11): Sand 52, Lahn 45.
Through Oct 14 Sand had $5.35 million on hand to Lahn's $403,000; about 70% of Lahn's money came from an RGA-affiliated PAC.
Lahn's residency history was a line of attack at the first debate. Sand pulled out of the Oct 21 debate after a death in his family; a new date is being sought.
research.ballot: Rob Sand (D), Zach Lahn (R). Gov. Kim Reynolds is not running.

research.summary: Mazzei is favored, but Republicans have not fully united behind him after a runoff he won by about 2,000 votes.
points: The only public poll, Cross Timbers (Oct 7 to 12), is an opt-in panel of 91 likely voters with a 15-point margin of error: Mazzei 39, Munson 36, independent Jerry Griffin 7.
Only 55% of registered Republicans back Mazzei in that poll, against 87% of Democrats for Munson. Gov. Stitt's approval is 32 to 55.
Mazzei would eliminate the state income tax; Munson runs on public schools and costs.
research.ballot: Mike Mazzei (R), Cyndi Munson (D), independents Jerry Griffin, Robert E. Brooks Sr. and Orlando Lynn Bush.
research.adjustment_note: Considered and not made: the signs of a close race all come from one very small poll the model already counts.

research.summary: Rated Lean D, but every independent poll since mid-September has it within 2 points.
points: DHM for OPB (Sep 17 to 27): Drazan 46, Kotek 44. DHM for The Oregonian (Sep 24 to Oct 1): Kotek 46, Drazan 44. Kotek's own pollster (Oct 1 to 4): Kotek 46, Drazan 42.
52% name cost of living, housing, taxes or jobs as the state's top problem; fewer than 30% say Oregon is on the right track.
Kotek has more than $8 million on hand to Drazan's under $1 million. Drazan led most polls in 2022 too, and Kotek won by 3.5.
research.ballot: Tina Kotek (D, incumbent), Christine Drazan (R), Brett Smith (Pacific Green).
research.adjustment_reason: Only one polling average reached the poll file, so the model gives Oregon's polls about a quarter of the weight other states' polls get and, left alone, would sit near Kotek +8, while the independent polls average a tie. Moved 2 points toward the Republicans, the cap.

research.method: Read by hand from local and national reporting on each competitive race. Notes describe the race; they do not move the forecast. An adjustment is made only where the reporting shows something the Cook rating and the polling on file do not yet carry, it is never more than 2 points of margin, and it is dropped automatically if this file is not re-researched within three weeks.

indicators.label: Gas price
indicators.context: Weekly U.S. regular all-formulations retail average.
indicators.why: The most visible price in America, posted on every corner. Gas spikes track closely with presidential approval and are the clearest way a war abroad lands in voters' budgets.

indicators.label: Oil (WTI)
indicators.context: West Texas Intermediate spot price, with Brent for comparison.
indicators.why: The upstream driver of the gas price and of the energy line in CPI. Shown for context; its effect is counted through gas and inflation, not twice.

indicators.label: Inflation (CPI)
indicators.context: Headline CPI, all urban consumers, versus the same month a year earlier.
indicators.why: Cost of living is the top issue for nearly half of registered voters in every party. Inflation sank Democrats in 2022 despite a strong job market.

indicators.label: Consumer sentiment
indicators.context: University of Michigan Index of Consumer Sentiment, 1966 = 100.
indicators.why: How people feel about their own finances, not what GDP says. Sentiment moves with approval and is a leading read on turnout mood.

indicators.label: Real wage growth
indicators.context: Average hourly earnings growth minus CPI inflation, both year over year.
indicators.why: Paychecks that lose ground to prices are the core of the 'wrong track' mood. Income growth is one of the oldest predictors of how the president's party fares.

indicators.label: Unemployment
indicators.context: Unemployment rate with the latest month's change in nonfarm payrolls.
indicators.why: Joblessness is low by historical standards, which blunts economic anger - but hiring has been weak most of the year.

indicators.label: GDP growth
indicators.context: Real GDP, percent change from the preceding quarter at an annual rate.
indicators.why: Background condition more than a voting issue; slow growth plus high prices is the stagflation mix that erodes support for the party in power.

indicators.label: 30-yr mortgage rate
indicators.context: Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey, 30-year fixed.
indicators.why: Housing costs rank second only to health care among costs voters want Congress to address. Higher rates lock younger voters out of buying.

indicators.label: 10-yr Treasury yield
indicators.context: Constant-maturity Treasury yields; the 2-year tracks Fed expectations.
indicators.why: Voters don't watch bond yields, but yields set mortgage, auto and card rates, and a Fed hike eight weeks before an election is a headline risk.

indicators.label: S&P 500
indicators.context: S&P 500 closing level, with the year-to-date return.
indicators.why: Matters most to the roughly 6 in 10 households with market exposure through 401(k)s. A weak link to midterm results on its own, but a falling market in October feeds the bad-news cycle.

political.label: Trump job approval
political.context: Average of 9 public approval aggregators as collated on Wikipedia.
political.why: The single strongest predictor of midterm losses. Since WWII the president's party has lost House seats in all but two midterms (1998, 2002), and presidents under 50% approval have lost about 37 seats on average (Gallup).

sources.name: Wikipedia: opinion polling on the second Trump presidency

political.label: Iran war: support / oppose
political.context: US and Israeli strikes began Feb 28, 2026. Reuters/Ipsos late August. A Politico poll found 61% say the war has raised their household costs.
political.why: Unpopular wars have hurt the president's party in past midterms (1950, 2006), and this one runs straight through the gas pump.

sources.name: Al Jazeera on the war and the midterms, Sept 4 2026

political.label: Cost of living on wrong track
political.context: Reuters/Ipsos via Marketplace. Voters most want Congress to tackle health care, housing, then groceries. Trust on the economy is split: 37% Democrats, 36% Republicans.
political.why: Shows the economic mood is anger at the status quo rather than enthusiasm for the opposition, which is why the economy tilts the race without deciding it on its own.
